passage:
Dalia had noticed it by her third month at the Rotterdam studio: nobody picked a colour anymore. They made three versions and waited for Elif. Elif chose the blue, moved the logo two millimetres, rewrote the email to the printer. At Thursday stand-ups Joost said 'whatever Elif thinks' so often it had become a joke no one laughed at.
The museum poster went out nine days late. Dalia didn't say Elif was controlling. She brought the calendar instead.
'On the last two jobs, most of the delay was work sitting in the approval pile,' she said. 'If we decide type and colour inside the brand guide, and you review the final draft only, I think we'd hit our dates.'
Elif studied the calendar for a long moment. 'Show me one job done that way.'

qa.q: How late did the museum poster go out?
What did Dalia think was really slowing the studio down?
qa.a: She thought the delays came from work sitting in the approval pile, because the team had stopped choosing and waited for Elif.

qa.q: Why did Dalia choose to bring the calendar instead of calling Elif controlling?
qa.a: The dates kept the talk on results that Elif could check rather than on Elif's character, and that made a trial possible.

qa.q: How might Elif feel being shown the calendar instead of being called controlling?
qa.a: Elif might feel less attacked and more able to weigh the idea, since the dates are facts to check; 'Show me one job done that way' suggests cautious openness.

grounding: Shows a team watching Elif decide every detail, the resulting delays and passivity, and feedback framed around results rather than personality.

passage:
Every Monday at the district library, Irfan handed out a typed sheet: which books go on the front shelf, which chair the storyteller sits in, even what colour paper for the craft table. Simran, who ran the children's corner with two others, watched her colleagues stop bringing ideas. Kusum used to invent puppet voices; now she read the sheet aloud and went home on time.
Saturday storytime, once packed with thirty kids, had shrunk to about twelve.
Simran waited for the monthly meeting. 'Sir, can I show you the sign-in book? Attendance was highest in the months we tried new formats. Could each of us plan one Saturday a month, and you look at the numbers after?'
Irfan frowned at the register, then turned a page back, and another. 'One Saturday,' he said. 'We'll see.'

qa.q: How many kids came to Saturday storytime before it shrank?
qa.a: It was once packed with thirty kids and shrank to about twelve.

qa.q: What does Kusum reading the sheet aloud and going home on time suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels discouraged and has given up offering her own ideas, perhaps sensing they would not count under the typed sheets.

qa.q: What choice did Simran make at the monthly meeting, and why might it work?
qa.a: She showed Irfan the sign-in book and asked for each person to plan one Saturday; tying the request to attendance, not to his style, made him willing to try.

qa.q: How might Irfan see his typed sheets after turning back through the register?
qa.a: Irfan may start to wonder whether the sheets cost the library its crowds; 'One Saturday' suggests cautious openness.

grounding: Shows a staff member watching a leader decide every detail, colleagues losing initiative and attendance falling, and feedback built on results.
